source_neutral.procedure: The object acted on is the time-varying sequence of waiting cases at each approval handoff. A single slow case or a single queue snapshot cannot distinguish persistent accumulation from a temporary surge. The procedure assumes ticket histories can identify when a case becomes ready for approval and when approval begins or finishes; the meanings of those timestamps and the ownership of each handoff are to be verified before monitoring starts. If approval-start timestamps are unavailable, ready-to-decision elapsed time is measured instead, and it is explicitly kept on record that this measure mixes waiting time with approval work time. The overall process is a proposed four-week baseline monitoring phase followed, if the evidence supports a candidate handoff, by a four-week pilot of one bounded change. Both durations are provisional and are not established as adequate. The same measurements and comparison rules are used in both phases, with review at the scheduled pilot end.
source_neutral.action: 1) At the same time each working day, record for each handoff: waiting count, ages of pending cases, arrivals and departures. 2) Weekly, summarize median and upper-tail ready-to-approval elapsed times, and show unresolved cases separately so that slow unfinished cases are not omitted. 3) Keep definitions and sampling times fixed, compare like case types, and annotate demand, staffing, exceptions and workflow changes. 4) Before judging any pattern, specify a minimum case count, a practically meaningful change threshold, and an expected-variation range, using service targets where available and baseline variation. 5) Use three consecutive weekly summaries beyond the relevant range or threshold as a provisional persistence rule. 6) If a handoff shows persistent excess elapsed time together with an aging or growing queue under comparable conditions, inspect that handoff's exceptions and ownership records. 7) Where those records suggest unclear assignment, pilot one bounded change: automatic assignment of eligible cases to a named approver on arrival, limited to one handoff and one case type. 8) During the pilot, apply the same measurements and comparison rules, and retain a comparable unchanged group if feasible. 9) Audit suspect records, mark affected comparisons as unreliable, and record concurrent changes.
source_neutral.observables: Baseline phase: repeated elevation, progressive increase, reversal, or threshold crossing in handoff elapsed times and pending-case ages, supported by queue counts and by imbalance between arrivals and departures. Candidate accumulation is located where these patterns persist within comparable case types, as opposed to appearing only in an aggregate average. Pilot phase: a sustained reduction beyond the predefined change threshold and the expected-variation range, together with reduced pending-case ages. Also monitored against predefined acceptable limits: downstream queue ages, end-to-end turnaround, and approval error or rework rates; these distinguish local improvement from delay displaced to later stages or from degraded outcomes. Supporting records: annotations of demand, staffing, exceptions and workflow changes; unresolved cases reported separately; exception and ownership records for the flagged handoff; the comparable unchanged group where one is retained.
source_neutral.inferential_warrant: Persistent patterns that agree across measures support identifying a handoff as a location of observed delay accumulation; isolated peaks support less confidence. Trends and reversals constrain whether the accumulation appears sustained, worsening or resolving. An exception pattern related to ownership makes explicit assignment a candidate remedy, not an established cause. Sustained pilot improvement under comparable demand and staffing, without downstream or quality deterioration, supports retaining the change within the tested scope. Improvement relative to a comparable unchanged group strengthens that assessment but does not by itself establish causality. If counts are inadequate, conditions become incomparable, or results remain within expected variation, the assessment is reported as inconclusive. Queue growth alone can reflect increased demand. Ready-to-decision time cannot isolate waiting without approval-start data. Interviews and ownership records suggest mechanisms but do not establish the contributions of stages that are not directly observed. Conclusions are restricted to the observed conditions.
source_neutral.problem_decomposition: Units: individual approval handoffs; case types within each handoff; individual cases with ready, approval-start and approval-finish or decision timestamps; daily samples taken at a fixed time; weekly summaries; resolved versus unresolved cases; the baseline phase and the pilot phase; the piloted handoff and case type versus a comparable unchanged group where feasible; downstream stages and the end-to-end flow. Quantities per handoff: waiting count, pending-case ages, arrivals, departures, median and upper-tail elapsed times. Relationships: elapsed-time and pending-age patterns are read together with queue counts and arrival-departure imbalance; comparisons are made within like case types and under comparable demand and staffing, not across an aggregate average; ready-to-decision time is a composite of waiting and approval work when approval-start data are missing; local change at the piloted handoff is checked against downstream queue ages, end-to-end turnaround, and error or rework rates; patterns are judged relative to the pre-specified minimum case count, change threshold, expected-variation range and three-consecutive-week persistence rule; ownership and exception records link a flagged handoff to the candidate change of automatic assignment to a named approver.
source_neutral.next_inquiry: When a handoff shows persistent excess elapsed time with an aging or growing queue under comparable conditions, inspect its exceptions and ownership records; where these suggest unclear assignment, run the bounded automatic-assignment pilot on one handoff and one case type. Review at the scheduled pilot end. If the assessment is inconclusive (inadequate counts, incomparable conditions, or results within expected variation), specify a revised monitoring period before another assessment. If adequate monitoring shows no meaningful benefit, revert the pilot and inspect exceptions before selecting another bounded change. Where records are suspect, audit them and resume assessment only with comparable measurements. Before broader rollout or stronger causal claims, seek a longer comparable series or a separately scoped controlled pilot.
source_neutral.limits: Conditions that can create or conceal temporal patterns: timestamp errors, inconsistent definitions, censoring from unresolved cases, regression to the mean after an unusually bad period, missed samples, changing case mix or staffing, and concurrent interventions. Affected comparisons are marked unreliable, and assessment resumes only with comparable measurements. The proposed intervals, thresholds and persistence rule may miss short disruptions or mistake seasonal variation for change; successive weekly observations may be correlated; four weeks per phase may therefore be insufficient, and both phase durations and the persistence rule are provisional. Queue growth alone can reflect increased demand. Ready-to-decision time cannot isolate waiting without approval-start data. Interviews and ownership records suggest mechanisms but do not establish the contributions of unobserved stages. A comparable unchanged group is retained only if feasible, and improvement against it does not by itself establish causality. Conclusions are restricted to observed conditions and to the tested scope of one handoff and one case type. Entry condition for the pilot: baseline evidence supports a candidate, and exception and ownership records suggest unclear assignment. Stopping rules: review at the scheduled pilot end; stop and revert earlier if a predefined downstream or quality limit is breached; revert the pilot if adequate monitoring shows no meaningful benefit; report as inconclusive and set a revised monitoring period if counts are inadequate, conditions become incomparable, or results remain within expected variation.
